This is NPR News Now.
The latest headlines every hour.
Live from NPR News in Washington, I'm Corva Coleman. The midterm elections are a little more than a week away. President Trump leaves today for Mississippi, where he'll campaign for Republican candidates.
GOP party officials worked to redraw some congressional districts in the past couple of years to help GOP candidates who want to keep control of the U.S. Congress.
But NPR's Tamara Keith reports, even if a district is drawn to reflect one party's successes in prior elections, it doesn't mean they'll win the next.
Some of these lines were drawn based on the Trump 2024 electorate, which was a real high watermark.
Since then, key pieces of the Trump base have soured on the president, including young voters and Latino voters.
The president's approval rating is now at a new low. A number of Democratic incumbents who were directly targeted in the new maps decided to stick it out and fight.
NPR's Tamara Keith reporting.
Weather forecasters say there is still catastrophic flooding happening in the Four Corners region of the Southwest.
That's Arizona, Colorado, New Mexico and Utah.
Extremely heavy rain triggered the flooding on the San Juan River. San Juan County officials in Northwest New Mexico are telling residents not to enter homes in the region.
From member station KUNM in Albuquerque, Megan Kamrick reports.
County undersheriff Corey Tanner says hidden hazards include raw sewage and chemicals in the water, as well as damaged utility infrastructure.
He urges residents to be patient so authorities can go house by house to check for hazards.
As far as we know, we've got through this without any significant injury or deaths.
You've got to help us. We don't want that to be someone walking into a house and flipping on a light switch with a gas leak.
New Mexico Governor Michelle Lujan Grisham is seeking a federal emergency disaster declaration.
Another round of storms could hit the region later this week.
For NPR News, I'm Megan Kamrick in Albuquerque.
Iran is bracing for a return to war after the U.S. midterm election next week.
The U.S. and Israel have said this round of strikes may be fiercer than the last two.
And Piazz Hadil Al-Shantji reports.
Iran is striking a defiant tone, as the U.S. and Israel say they're preparing to resume strikes after the midterm elections.
Iran's Foreign Ministry spokesperson Ismail Bakhrai said that Iran has, quote, "never left the negotiating table," but is also prepared for war.
President Trump has claimed that Iran's military infrastructure was destroyed, but Iran has come back forcefully in the past.
Iran expert Trita Parsi of the Quincy Institute for Responsible Statecraft says Trump underestimates Iran.
Even if its arsenal has been depleted, its capacity to rebuild and produce missiles and other forms of munitions is very, very formidable.
He says Tehran wants to make the cost of a new conflict so high that Washington has to back down.
Hadil Al-Shantji, NPR News, Istanbul.
You're listening to NPR.
Brazil's incumbent President Luis Anacio Lula da Silva has won re-election.
He came back from second place in Brazil's first round of voting to defeat right-wing Senator Flavio Bolsonaro in yesterday's final round.
Bolsonaro is the son of the country's former far-right president.
There were enormous protests over the weekend in France by people angry over school conditions and the rising cost of living.
High school students originally began these protests, demanding that the French government spend more on their needs.
In Serbia yesterday, a student-led slate of candidates toppled the incumbent government.
That includes Serbia's long-serving leader.
Other European protests have happened in Albania, Italy, Spain, and Portugal.
Students in the U.S. are still missing more school than before the pandemic.
N.P.S. Janaki Mehta reports on the latest.
We'll start with the good news.
More students have been coming to school regularly in the last few years.
But attendance still isn't where it was before the pandemic.
That's all in a new report from five organizations that focus on chronic absenteeism.
And the reasons for absences have changed.
For example, families are more cautious about sickness since COVID.
Recent immigration crackdowns have led some parents to keep their kids at home.
And students also report feeling less connected when they're at school.
Building strong relationships with students, making class more engaging,
and making sure there's reliable transportation are among some of the strategies schools can use to keep improving attendance.
Janaki Mehta, NPR News.
You're listening to NPR News from Washington.
